# Part A - Creating Data Frames

# Question #1

Create a data frame
```{r}
survey <- data.frame(
  Respondents        = 1:20,
  Sex                = c(2,2,1,2,2,2,2,2,2,2,1,2,2,2,2,2,2,2,1,2),
  Fathers_Occupation = c(1,3,3,3,1,2,3,1,1,1,3,2,1,3,3,1,3,1,2,1),
  Persons_at_Home    = c(5,7,3,8,5,9,6,7,8,4,7,5,4,7,8,8,3,11,7,6),
  Siblings_at_School = c(6,4,4,1,2,1,5,3,1,2,3,2,5,5,2,1,2,5,3,2),
  Types_of_Houses    = c(1,2,3,1,1,3,3,1,2,3,2,3,2,2,3,3,3,3,3,2)
)
survey
```

Subset it
```{r}
survey[survey$Sex == 1, ]
survey[survey$Persons_at_Home > 6, ]
survey[, c("Sex", "Types_of_Houses")]
```

Inspect its properties
```{r}
str(survey)
dim(survey)
names(survey)
summary(survey)
head(survey)
```

Recode it
```{r}
survey$Sex <- factor(survey$Sex, levels = 1:2,
                     labels = c("Male", "Female"))
survey$Fathers_Occupation <- factor(survey$Fathers_Occupation, levels = 1:3,
                                    labels = c("Farmer", "Driver", "Others"))
survey$Types_of_Houses <- factor(survey$Types_of_Houses, levels = 1:3,
                                 labels = c("Wood", "Semi-Concrete", "Concrete"))
str(survey)
```

Analyze it
```{r}
table(survey$Sex)
table(survey$Fathers_Occupation)
table(survey$Types_of_Houses)
table(survey$Sex, survey$Types_of_Houses)
mean(survey$Persons_at_Home)
mean(survey$Siblings_at_School)
tapply(survey$Persons_at_Home, survey$Types_of_Houses, mean)
```

survey <- data.frame(Respondent, Sex, FathersOccupation, PersonsAtHome, SiblingsAtSchool, TypesOfHouses)

# Question #2

Every row in the data frame stands for one respondent, so all six columns need exactly 20 entries to keep each person's answers together. If a vector were shorter or longer, data.frame() would either stop with an error or pair answers with the wrong respondents, which would make the whole data set unreliable.

# Question #3

Sex, FathersOccupation, and TypesOfHouses are nominal data, since their numbers only stand for the categories listed in the legend. PersonsAtHome and SiblingsAtSchool are true counts of people. Averaging Sex would be misleading because a value like 1.85 describes no one, and it would change if the codes were swapped even though the respondents stayed the same.

# Question #4

```{r}
survey <- survey_raw
survey[survey$Sex == 1, ]
```

Filtering with Sex == 1 returns the correct rows, but the output only shows 1s with no hint of what they stand for. Someone without the legend could read 1 as female, male, or something else entirely, and the other coded columns would be just as confusing. This shows that coded data is hard to interpret until it is converted into labeled factors.

# Question #5

```{r}
nrow(survey[survey$Sex == 1, ])
sum(survey$Sex == 1)
```

Only 3 of the 20 respondents are male, so the sample is heavily lopsided (3 males versus 17 females). With so few cases, one or two respondents can change a pattern a lot, so I would not be confident generalizing any finding to a larger population.

# Question #6

```{r}
summary(survey)
```

summary() reports a minimum, mean, and maximum for Sex and TypesOfHouses because they are stored as plain numbers, and R treats a numeric column as a quantity unless told otherwise (for example with factor()). This shows that how data is stored is different from what it means, so the analyst has to supply the meaning.

# Question #7

```{r}
mean(survey$PersonsAtHome)
mean(survey$Sex)
```

The mean of PersonsAtHome (6.4) is meaningful because it is a real count and represents the average household size in the sample. The mean of Sex (1.85) is not, because 1 and 2 are only labels, so the number describes no group and would change if the codes were swapped.
